transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I just feel restless all the time, like there’s a motor running inside me. If I have to sit still—like at church, here at the clinic, or even at home—I start feeling trapped, and I need to get up or do something.
Have you started or changed the dose of any medications recently, especially any antipsychotic or anti-nausea drugs?
I don’t think so. I haven’t started anything new or changed any doses that I know of.
When you feel this restlessness, is it mainly in your legs with an urge to move them, or is it more of a general feeling of inner tension throughout your whole body?

It’s more my whole body, like an inside motor that won’t shut off. Not just my legs. If I’m sitting in church, here, or even at home, I start feeling trapped and like I have to get up or do something.
Along with this restless feeling, do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of different things—like your health, family, or work—on most days?

I’m not sure I’d call it worrying like that. I mean, I think about stuff, but it’s not like I’m sitting there most days worrying about my health or family or work. It feels more like restlessness than worry.
Have you noticed any recent periods where you felt unusually elevated, euphoric, or irritable, along with needing much less sleep than usual but still feeling energetic?
No, I haven’t noticed anything like that. I don’t get those times where I’m feeling really up or needing way less sleep and still full of energy.
Did you notice this kind of restlessness back when you were a child or teenager, or is this something that started more recently, as an adult?
It goes way back. When I was a boy in school, teachers were always moving my seat because I couldn’t stay put. I’d talk out of turn and get in trouble for jumping up before class was done.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient reports a lifelong pattern (since childhood) of motor restlessness, inability to remain seated, impulsive interrupting, and being frequently moved by teachers for disruptive hyperactivity—classic hyperactive-impulsive symptoms. Current symptoms (whole-body 'inner motor,' need to move, feeling trapped when still) represent an adult continuation of this same trait rather than a new-onset anxiety or mood disturbance. Generalized anxiety was explicitly denied (no excessive worry about health/family/work), manic/hypomanic episodes were denied, and no recent antipsychotic exposure or focal leg-only urge to move (which would suggest akathisia or restless legs) was present. The chronic, early-onset, pervasive hyperactive-impulsive pattern best fits ADHD, predominantly hyperactive-impulsive presentation.
